scope_honesty_assessment.assessment: This is the right limitation to declare for a normalising comparator - over-broad normalisation is exactly the way such a tool goes vacuous, and the producer both names the risk and mitigates it by emitting the normalisation inventory. My stub probe confirms the mitigation is real: removing a normalisation rule breaks the tests, so the rules are pinned rather than free-floating. The producer did not anticipate the HC-B self-inflicted false positive.

reproducibility_check: The real double clone was run in a fresh python3 -I process; byte_equivalent=true reproduced, and normalized_fields was identical for both clones (12 and 12).
disposition_reason: The PASS is justified and the evidence is not synthetic-only. I independently reproduced the frozen hypothesis at a larger commit than the producer used - 12 real test files, byte-equivalent, both clones clean, with only unittest elapsed duration normalised - and I verified the producer's cited commit and its 8-test-file count are both real rather than asserted. The tests survive three stub substitutions including removal of the second clone and removal of a normalisation rule, so the normalisation is pinned and cannot silently broaden. Accepted with one defect logged: HC-B shows a self-inflicted false positive from naming the clones 'clone-a' and 'clone-b', which makes a deterministic suite that prints its own root basename look non-deterministic.
followups_for_coordinator: double_clone_runner names its clones 'clone-a' and 'clone-b' under one workspace, and normalize() rewrites only the full clone path. A committed test printing Path.cwd().name therefore yields byte_equivalent=false for a fully deterministic suite (reviewer-observed: 'clone-a' vs 'clone-b'). Use an identical basename under two distinct parent directories.

When byte_equivalent is false the report does not name the diverging observable; the reader must diff canonical_results. A diverging-field summary would make the negative case as legible as the positive one.
